title: Shell company red flags: how to check and weigh each one
summary: A crowded address or a busy director proves little on its own. What each red flag is evidence of, how to check it against a primary source, and what it means…
body_markdown:
The common ones are a registered address shared with many other companies, directors who sit on large numbers of boards, a filing history with no sign of trading, a website or phone number much younger than the business claims to be, ownership that runs through other companies without reaching a person, and no trace of staff, premises or customers. Each has ordinary explanations, so they carry most weight when several independent flags agree and contradict what the company says about itself.


Compare what the company says it does with what the public record shows. Read the registry's filing history and accounts for signs of trading, count the other companies at its registered address and on its directors' appointment lists, date its website and phone number, and look for staff, customers and suppliers who have dealt with it. A company that claims years of trading but filed dormant accounts and registered its domain this year has a specific question to answer.


Yes, many. Companies with no operations of their own are used to hold shares in operating subsidiaries, to complete mergers, to run joint ventures, to separate liabilities and to hold personal or family assets. That is why being a shell is not a finding on its own. The useful question is whether the company's shape fits what it says it does.


A shell company has no independent operations, significant assets, ongoing business activities or employees. A front company is a functioning business with the look of a legitimate one, used to disguise illicit financial activity. Checks for shells look for missing operations, while checks for fronts look for activity that does not fit the money passing through.


A person who appears as a director on a company's records and in the registry while someone else directs the company. Some are professionals supplied by formation agents and sit on large numbers of boards, and others are relatives or associates of the real controller. A long appointment list is worth reading closely, but many belong to company secretaries, accountants and directors of large groups.


Usually because a formation agent, accountant or virtual office provides the registered office for its clients, so one address can host thousands of companies. That tells you a service provider is involved. It becomes more telling when the companies at the address share officers, phone numbers and formation dates with the one you are reviewing.
